title: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA and DuckLabs released Sirius, an open-source GPU-native SQL engine from UW–Madison and NVIDIA, as a DuckDB core extension that runs supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs with two SQL commands and CPU fallback. NVIDIA's cold-run TPC-H-derived benchmarks on AWS (SF100 to SF10K, data in Amazon S3) show tuned two-GPU Sirius delivering 3.25x–5.50x speedups and up to ~79% lower query-time compute cost versus the best tested CPU DuckDB configurations, with caveats on methodology.

themes.theme: GPU acceleration enters the DuckDB ecosystem as a drop-in extension

insights.claim: NVIDIA and DuckLabs released Sirius, an open-source GPU-native SQL engine developed by the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, as an official DuckDB core extension that accelerates supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Distribution through an embedded analytics database's core extension channel widens NVIDIA's GPU demand surface into everyday SQL analytics, beyond AI training.
insights.quote: NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release Sirius as a DuckDB core extension, bringing GPU acceleration to DuckDB’s analytical query engine.
insights.locator: NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release

insights.claim: Sirius GPU acceleration in DuckDB is enabled with two SQL commands (INSTALL sirius and LOAD sirius) and requires no SQL rewrites, no schema changes, and no separate GPU programming API.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Near-zero switching cost lowers the adoption barrier for GPU analytics, which is a key driver of incremental data-center GPU consumption.
insights.quote: without rewriting your SQL or changing database schemas
insights.locator: NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release

insights.claim: In the Sirius DuckDB integration, DuckDB keeps SQL parsing and optimization while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU as a whole, and queries with unsupported features automatically fall back to DuckDB's CPU engine.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: The hybrid CPU-fallback design reduces operational risk for adopters, but also signals Sirius does not yet cover the full SQL feature set.
insights.quote: Sirius accelerates supported queries as a whole. DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU.
insights.locator: Accelerate DuckDB queries without rewriting SQL

insights.claim: The Sirius DuckDB extension requires DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver, is roughly a 700 MB download, and automatically selects the CUDA backend for the installed driver.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Dependence on CUDA keeps GPU-accelerated DuckDB analytics locked to NVIDIA hardware, reinforcing the CUDA software moat.

themes.theme: Benchmark claims: speed and compute-cost gains at terabyte scale

insights.claim: In NVIDIA's cold-run TPC-H-derived benchmarks with data in Amazon S3, tuned Sirius on AWS instances with two NVIDIA GPUs delivered 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configurations.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Multi-x speedups on standard analytics benchmarks support the case that GPUs can displace CPU cycles in cloud data warehousing workloads.
insights.quote: delivered 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configurations
insights.locator: With tuned settings, Sirius running on

insights.claim: At TPC-H scale factor 1,000 (1 TB), tuned two-GPU Sirius cut total query runtime from 347.3 seconds on the best CPU DuckDB setup to 63.2 seconds, and at SF3K (3 TB) from 752.4 to 160.6 seconds (4.69x) with roughly 71% lower query-time compute cost.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Concrete runtime and cost numbers give a basis for estimating CPU-to-GPU substitution economics in cloud analytics.
insights.locator: With tuned settings, Sirius running on

insights.claim: At TPC-H scale factor 10,000 (10 TB), tuned two-GPU Sirius completed the workload in 729.9 seconds versus 2,369.4 seconds for the best CPU-based DuckDB configuration, a 3.25x speedup with about 79% lower query-time compute cost — the largest cost advantage measured.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: The cost advantage of GPU analytics appears to grow with data scale, favoring GPU adoption in the largest (most lucrative) analytics workloads.
insights.quote: The largest cost advantage appeared at SF10K.
insights.locator: The largest cost advantage appeared at SF10K

insights.claim: The Sirius benchmark methodology favors the GPU in some respects: it used pinned development builds, Sirius timings excluded result fetch/export while DuckDB timings included CSV output, and compute costs excluded startup, validation, storage, S3, and idle time.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Vendor benchmark asymmetries mean real-world total-cost-of-ownership gains are likely smaller than headline numbers; discount accordingly.
insights.quote: Sirius timings exclude result fetch/export, while DuckDB timings include CSV output.
insights.locator: We evaluated Sirius against CPU-based DuckDB

themes.theme: Configuration and tuning matter more as workloads scale

insights.claim: Optimal GPU configuration for Sirius depends on workload size: at TPC-H SF100 a single GPU gave the lowest cost while two GPUs gave the shortest runtime, whereas at SF10K the tuned two-GPU setup beat the tuned single-GPU setup on both runtime and cost.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Larger analytics datasets push buyers toward multi-GPU instances, raising GPU attach per workload as data volumes grow.
insights.quote: The results also show how workload size affects configuration choices.
insights.locator: The results also show how workload

insights.claim: Tuning is critical for Sirius at large scale: at TPC-H SF10K the default two-GPU configuration did not finish, while the tuned configuration completed in 729.9 seconds.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Out-of-the-box robustness gaps at 10 TB scale indicate GPU SQL engines still need expert tuning, a friction point for enterprise adoption.

insights.claim: NVIDIA cautions that Sirius performance results will vary with query structure, dataset size, hardware, and cache conditions, and publishes a benchmark runner and configurations in the Sirius repository for independent evaluation.
insights.speaker: Allison Ding
insights.so_what: Open, reproducible benchmarks allow third-party validation, which will determine whether GPU analytics claims hold outside vendor tests.
insights.quote: Results will vary with query structure, dataset size, hardware, and cache conditions.
